If I may put a long quote by an acquaintance that tried (and is still trying) to get a video aggregation site running, he had it for a month, but issue arise when the people who want you dead are persistent:

"Of the total "registered users" only a fragment were ever "active" more than just setting up a channel. However, I had been told for years that the website was supported entirely on ad revenue and money coming in from various "successful lawsuits" against all manner of people and corporations. I was an idiot and believed it- knowing what I know now, cranking even $50 a month out of adsense is a challenge. You can't base a site like that on ads alone. I sure didn't!

As for disk space, Alisson is again 110% correct. MetaJolt's general bill was about $400 a month, with nearly 2/3rds of that just going for our storage server. Hard disk space, especially fast network storage for things like video playback, is very expensive. Likewise, you have to build it smart with expansion in mind, or you can run out of room in your physical server for more drives. It's an ugly catch 22. The other killer that no one talks about is bandwidth- every second of video delivered through the connection to the end user costs money- you have to have enough space allocated, or it costs you BIG TIME. Now, picture this- you have a 750MB file that not only has to be stored, but you have to pay for 750MB of video to be delivered "X" number of times- which will eat through most "stock" server bandwidth plans in a couple of days. That's why getting the right host is critical when you're looking at starting one of these up- getting the best bandwidth package possible is truly make or break, with the break not only shutting you down but also hitting you with overage charges into the hundreds (or even thousands) of dollars.

MetaJolt got around these problems a few ways- I'm happy to explain them because anyone taking a crack at this market deserves to know how to make a proper go of it. First, you have to throttle back upload limits. Ours was 100MB for a long time, with our "high" for 2016 planned to be around 550MB for a total file size. The total per-user limit of 1GB per week was plotted to be raised to 2GB per week, with a third "tier" proposed for some power users that met internal criteria to get 3GB a week. Most users never got even close to the weekly cap. This was vital so that we knew, at a glance, how much disk space we could go through per week. Multiply all the users by their maximum weekly allotment, and you've got a rough estimate of how far out to plan. Best advice I can give a new startup is start very slow. Unless you know exactly what you can afford and what you are doing, don't give more than you know you can lose.

Next one is kind of a cop out, but allow embeds. Seriously, that solved 90% of our uploader-related issues. Slow playback? Embed it. Too long? Embed it. Poor quality through our converter? Embed it. MetaJolt had a 5-to-1 ratio of embedded videos to uploaded videos, and that made all the difference in my mind.

Finally, find a host that is flexible. In MetaJolt's short existence, it's had a bevy of hosts, some good, some pretty lousy. Barring all the bogus legal claims made against us by a sociopath without a life, we had the best luck with a company called ReliableServers. I would recommend them to anyone starting one of these sites up- ask for Phil, he's great. Best bang for your buck, with a DDOS wall that's got an interface that's fun to watch. Not that there's some vengeful clown out there looking to close down all these sorts of sites because the video sharing market is "his market" of course, but just in case, a good DDOS wall never hurts." - Maklarr4000, former Zippcast staff, former MetaJolt staff.
